USPSTF Manuscript draft 

# Introduction

## Background

Problematic substance use represents a substantial and growing portion of the global disease burden, posing major challenges for health systems worldwide (Degenhardt et al., 2018; Whiteford et al., 2013). Despite the considerable public and private investment in prevention and treatment, substance-related problems continue to represent a major public health challenge (Barbosa et al., 2018). Within this context, tobacco, alcohol, and opioids remain the leading causes of preventable mortality (CDC, 2024a, 2024b; Gomes et al., 2018; GBD 2016 Alcohol Collaborators, 2018; GBD 2019 Tobacco Collaborators, 2021; Fang et al., 2025; Whiteford et al., 2013). This ongoing burden may partially reflect the limited long-term effectiveness of existing treatments. For example, 6-month abstinence rates for the most widely used smoking cessation pharmacotherapies range from 17.6% to 27.6% (Cahill et al., 2014).

Psychedelic treatments are demonstrating promise as responses to this crisis (Richard & Garcia-Romeu, 2025, Carhart-Harris & Goodwin, 2017; Nutt et al., 2020; Reiff et al., 2020). For example, there is emergent evidence of psychedelics’ efficacy for smoking cessation (Johnson, 2022; Johnson et al., 2026; Johnson et al., 2017; Glenn et al., 2025). In a recent randomized clinical trial, Johnson et al. (2026) found that those receiving psilocybin demonstrated six-fold greater odds of prolonged smoking abstinence at 6-months follow-up compared to those receiving a nicotine patch, a standard preventive intervention (OR=6.12, 1.99-23.26). Problematic alcohol use (AUD) may also be responsive (Andersen et al., 2021; Garcia-Romeu, et al., 2019); early trials indicate that psychedelic intervention involving psilocybin may reduce heavy drinking and daily drinking (Bogenschutz, 2022), and Sessa (2021) found 3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine-assisted psychotherapy (MDMA) to be safe and tolerable for patients with alcohol use disorder, contributing to reduced drinking as well. A scoping review found that in the majority of 40 studies addressing OUD, ibogaine, select derivatives and metabolites, and ketamine, could reduce opioid use, alleviate withdrawal symptoms, and change conditioned place preference (Pulido-Saavedra, et al., 2025). However, heterogeneity across the studies and various validity threats call for more rigorous study (Weleff, et al., 2025).

Observational studies reinforce these trial findings. In a prospective cohort study of community-referred people who use drugs, psychedelic use was associated with decreased odds of subsequent daily opioid use (AOR=0.45; 95%CI: 0.29 to 0.70) (Argento, 2021). A large cross-sectional online survey found that those with at least one lifetime psychedelic experience reported that the experience improved their health behaviors, including related to alcohol (66%) and tobacco (49%) and opioid use (40%); individuals engaging in more frequent use were more likely to report positive behavioral changes (Teixeira et al., 2025). 

## Preventive Care Meets Policy Gap

Despite promising findings around efficacy, even if approved by the United States (U.S.) Food & Drug Administration (FDA), implementation and economic models require further development (Marseille, Bertozzi & Kahn, 2022\) to guide their safe, scalable, and equitable integration into a fragmented U.S. healthcare system (Aday et al., 2023; Belouin et al., 2022; Marks & Cohen, 2021). Discourse regarding insurance coverage and payment feasibility is ongoing, with calls for Medicare reimbursement pathways to address cost-effectiveness (Propes et al., 2025; Marseille, Bertozzi & Kahn, 2022).

The epistemic frame shaping these deliberations will carry policy implications. For example, the current focus of psychedelic science and interventions is generally on treatment of behaviors that have already progressed to later stages. The subsequent narrowing of the scope of psychedelic service implementation, access, cost coverage and reimbursement limits the potential role of psychedelics in population health. A complementary public health frame takes the approach not of treating a problematic behavior but of preventing the adverse health outcomes associated with that behavior. While not dissimilar to the treatment of problematic behaviors, a prevention approach is nevertheless distinct as it expands the window for psychedelic interventions to earlier in behavior, health, and disease processes. Earlier, preventive measures are known to improve population health outcomes and reduce healthcare costs (Chen 2018; Masters, 2017; Musich, 2016; Maciosek et al., 2010). 

Additionally, in the United States, positioning psychedelic interventions within a prevention framework may also expand equitable access through a unique policy pathway. Specifically, Section 2713 of the U.S. Affordable Care Act (ACA) requires that private insurers cover recommended primary care preventive services without cost sharing (Koh & Sebelius, 2010). 

The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) issues these preventive services recommendations and is the body charged with establishing the sufficiency of the evidence base,largely through assessment of net benefits (benefits minus harms) (Fox & Shaw, 2015). Specifically, a USPSTF grade “A” (high certainty of substantial net benefit) or “B” (high certainty of moderate net benefit or moderate certainty of moderate or substantial net benefit) recommendation for a primary care-based prevention intervention for asymptomatic people can lead to the insurance coverage without cost sharing required under Section 2713 (Fox & Shaw, 2015). Although the USPSTF role has been challenged (see, for example, Kennedy v. Braidwood Management, Inc., 2025), the USPSTF currently still has a role in profoundly increasing access to preventive care. For example, they have issued recommendations for mammograms, HIV prophylaxis, and various smoking cessation interventions.

## The public health imperative of a prevention framework for psychedelics

While actions through the USPSTF are attributed with significant health protection and improvement, adverse population health consequences of tobacco, alcohol, and opioid use remain intractable, emphasizing the important advances psychedelic interventions could bring to preventive care. For example, tobacco cessation tools and interventions are critically important given smoking continues to be a major cause of preventable morbidity and mortality (GBD 2019 Tobacco Collaborators, 2021). In 2021, the USPSTF issued a grade A recommendation to FDA-approved tobacco-cessation pharmacotherapy and behavioral interventions (U.S. Preventive Services Task Force \[USPSTF\], 2021a), making it one of only four USPSTF-recommended pharmacotherapies as of this writing. However, these first-line interventions achieve only 17.6–27.6% six-month abstinence (Cahill et al., 2014), limiting their singular ability to significantly shift population health. 

With regards to either alcohol or opioid use disorders, the USPSTF currently makes no pharmacotherapy recommendations: the current Grade B recommendation for unhealthy alcohol use in adolescents and adults is limited to screening and brief behavioral counseling (USPSTF, 2018; 2025), and the 2020 Grade B recommendation for screening unhealthy drug use in adults explicitly notes that screen-detected populations show no benefit from brief counseling and that evidence for pharmacotherapy benefit is restricted to treatment-seeking populations (Krist et al., 2020). USPSTF does acknowledge the benefit and role of FDA-approved pharmacotherapies (naltrexone, methadone, buprenorphine) for opioid use disorder, but ultimately, there are no pharmacological preventive options assured of insurance coverage for two of the most lethal substance use conditions in adults (Degenhardt et al., 2018; Fang et al., 2025). Should the science concerning preventive psychedelic-assisted intervention continue to demonstrate effectiveness and be incorporated into the primary care setting, then psychedelics could fill a significant gap in preventive care and accessibility.

Further, psychedelics appear to produce concurrent improvements in depression, anxiety, well-being, and alcohol co-consumption (Garcia-Romeu et al., 2019; Raison et al., 2022; Teixeira et al., 2025). Although USPSTF's appraisal methodology evaluates each intervention independently, these co-benefits broaden the case for psychedelic-assisted prevention to produce population-level health impacts.

In this context, adding psychedelic interventions to the list of preventive measures could significantly improve population health. However, to our knowledge, psychedelic science has not incorporated a prevention frame in production of its evidence base, even as there are signs that the USPSTF may at some juncture turn their attention to psychedelics: The USPSTF’s draft Contextual Questions section of the *Research Plan for Tobacco Cessation in Adults: Interventions,* considered psilocybin (USPSTF, 2025), suggesting an emerging recognition and policy opportunity. 

The aims of this study are therefore to introduce how a public health prevention frame can apply to psychedelic interventions, highlighting population health implications and potential mechanisms of action. It then aims to open a policy window to expanded access and population benefits through this prevention frame by assessing how psychedelic research can evolve to meet USPSTF evidentiary standards. Our specific objectives are to evaluate the current body of psychedelic evidence relative to USPSTF criteria for its A or B rating and inform future research to better meet these standards as a policy pathway to greater and more equitable access.  

# Psychedelics in the context of prevention 

As illustrated in Figure 1, if psychedelic interventions were provided before the development (or onset) of problematic behaviors, then psychedelic-assisted interventions would function not just as treatments, but as primary or secondary prevention level modifiers of morbidity, and mortality, making them eligible for consideration by the USPSTF. 

#### Figure 1: The psychedelic prevention pathway for problematic substance use

![][image1]

In a seminal study exploring psychedelics’ preventive potential, addiction professionals agreed that psychedelics could function as preventive interventions rather than exclusively as treatment modalities (Lill, 2025). Clinical and observational data suggest psychedelics may be effective interventions for the primary and secondary prevention of adverse health outcomes linked to problematic smoking, alcohol, and opioid use. Bogenschutz (2022) found that psilocybin intervention was associated with decreased levels of the World Health Organization’s risk levels for alcohol, including improving blood pressure, the number one preventable risk factor for death worldwide. In individuals who use opioids, psychedelic use has been associated with a reduction in suicide risk among people who report at least one lifetime use of psychedelics and among individuals who use opioids (Teixeira, 2025; Argento et al., 2022), with Qeadan (2025) finding psychedelic use associated with fewer overdoses, relapses, mental health crises, and SUD-related hospitalizations or emergency department visits among people who use substances. Psychedelic use may also be associated with positive health outcomes among individuals with chronic pain, a condition that frequently co-occurs with and may contribute to problematic substance use; among adults using psychedelics to self-treat chronic pain, 78.8% reported improvements in physical health conditions, while 86.3% reported decreasing or ceasing use of at least one non-psychedelic substance, including 64.1% of those who had used prescription opioids (Glynos et al., 2025). These findings suggest that the potential preventive benefits of psychedelic interventions may extend beyond changes in substance use behavior to prevent adverse health outcomes associated with problematic substance use. Table 1 summarizes the behavioral targets of preventive psychedelic interventions and the health outcomes averted for smoking, alcohol use, and opioid use.

Psychedelic-assisted interventions may function in this preventive capacity by altering the trajectory from problematic behavior to health outcomes (Neuhaus & Slavich, 2022). Physiologically, psychedelic interventions have been linked to reduced drug cravings, which can also be critical to achieving cessation (Garcia-Romeu et al., 2017; Shen et al., 2025; Chapron et al., 2025). Psychedelic use may provide effective preventive care by enhancing flexibility and fluidity of cognition and thought patterns (Gattuso et al., 2022), loosening the influence of deeply held beliefs that guide behavior (Carhart-Harris & Friston, 2019). 

A psychological pathway for preventive behavior change may involve psychedelics’ role in reducing shame and self-stigmatization, well-known barriers to help-seeking behavior and maintenance of behavioral change in the context of substance use and substance use disorders (Hammarlund et al., 2018, Mathai et al., 2025). Additionally, psychedelic experiences may promote self-compassion and emotional processing, identity and self-perception revision, social connectedness, and enhanced psychological flexibility, potentially increasing capacity for “self-determination” and challenging the narratives and behaviors that influence substance use (Zeifman et al., 2025; Teixeira, 2022). Psychedelics also seem to enhance neuroplasticity and openness to change, which in turn support the disruption of entrenched patterns of psychological and behavioral rigidity. This disruption is necessary for sustained behavior modification and improved health outcomes (Neuhaus & Slavich, 2022; Nardou et al., 2023; Woodburn & Kwan, 2023).

Psychedelics may also prove effective as preventive agents because they treat mental health conditions that are risk factors for substance use disorders (Khantzian, 1997), even conferring transdiagnostic benefits. For example, childhood depressive disorders confer roughly twofold odds of subsequent SUD development across nicotine, alcohol, and other drugs (meta-analytic OR ≈ 2.0–2.6) (Groenman et al., 2017, Liang et al., 2022; McHugh & Weiss, 2019). Psychedelics have effectively improved depression and anxiety (Ko et al., 2023; Raison et al., 2023; Raison et al., 2022), including treatment-resistant depression (Carhart-Harris et al., 2016). 

At a population health level, psychedelic practices point to net benefits that are an important consideration in preventive care. Neither lifetime nor past use of psychedelics was associated with worse mental health status than seen among the general population, and in fact for many psychedelic substances it was associated with better (Krebs, 2013). A series of studies similarly found better health, substance use, lifestyle, and well-being status among those with routine intentional ayahuasca practices compared to the general population (Ona, 2019; Kohek, 2023; Teixeira, 2026).  

From a prevention science framework, these mechanisms suggest that the potential role for psychedelics to address tobacco, alcohol, and opioid use may especially align with primary and indicated prevention interventions that alter the trajectory of disorder onset and perhaps even initiation. Even if it is early to draw definitive conclusions from psychedelic science (Mackey, 2022), it is not too early for the frame of psychedelic scholarship to include prevention. 

# Methods

This study employs a “policy backward” framework to assess the requirements for a forward-facing research roadmap to psychedelics as preventive care, with a focus on the USPSTF. The methodology is divided into three distinct parts to bridge the gap between current clinical evidence and federal prevention policy: 1\) Literature review and evidence characterization, 2\) Data preparation, and 3\) Comparison with USPSTF methodological standards, screening/net benefit framework, and Category A/B benchmarks.

## Part 1: Literature Review and Characterization

The existing body of psychedelic research across tobacco, alcohol, and opioid domains was searched by drawing from data sources including PubMed, Scopus, Google Scholar, and AI-assisted search databases. Search queries include combinations of keywords referencing psychedelics broadly (e.g., psilocybin, LSD, ibogaine) and substance-related keywords for tobacco (“smoking”), alcohol (“drinking,” “AUD”), and opioid (“opiate,” “heroin,” “OUD”) use. We included clinical trials and observational studies that investigated the effects (or associations) of psychedelics with respect to substance use, craving, or recovery in human participants. While we included their constituent individual studies, we did not include pooled studies, only their constituent individual studies. 

## Part 2: Data Preparation

To evaluate the existing evidence for psychedelic-assisted therapies against USPSTF standards for Category A/B recommendations, we first reviewed the US Preventive Services Task Force Procedure Manual to identify their evidentiary standards and priorities. Subsequently, we created a codebook of 52 indicators across six domains: (1) Study Identification & Design (e.g., randomization, blinding, sample size, and validated measures); (2) Population & Generalizability (e.g., demographics and geographic settings); (3) Intervention & Safety (e.g., intervention delivery and adverse events); (4) Equity & Cultural Framing (e.g., Indigenous knowledge and community reciprocity); (5) Outcomes & Follow-Up (e.g., effect sizes and long-term behavioral endpoints. A sixth category, Substances, portrayed the distribution of research by specific substances used. While the indicators were developed for clinical trial standards, a subset also were measured for observational studies as part of the net benefit assessment (n, demographics, safety and efficacy).

### 2.1 Extraction procedure

Each included article was coded according to these indicators through a structured, AI-augmented two-step protocol. First, the full text of each article was submitted to Anthropic’s Claude Opus large language model using a fixed system prompt that instructed the model to function as an expert systematic reviewer with specialization in psychedelic science, substance-use disorders, and clinical-trial methodology. The model was required to return coded values exclusively as a single JSON object, organized according to the codebook’s variable order and response-type specifications. Second, selected outputs were reviewed and, when necessary, corrected by at least one of four human reviewers with formal training in epidemiology. Coding uncertainties and discrepancies were resolved through consensus-based discussion among the reviewer team.

Observational studies, including cohort studies, case series, case reports, and cross-sectional designs without a concurrent comparator arm, were not eligible for the clinical-trial coding pipeline described above and were therefore coded separately. These studies were assessed using a narrower, purpose-built codebook limited to adverse events, challenging experiences, and basic demographic characteristics. The resulting observational-study dataset was maintained as a standalone dataset and analyzed separately from, rather than merged with, the primary clinical-trial dataset. For each article, the source PDF was first converted to text through a deterministic preprocessing procedure, with optical character recognition used as a fallback when scanned articles did not yield usable text directly. Data extraction followed a one-article-per-model-call design: each article was assigned to an isolated model subagent and processed using Claude Sonnet 5 rather than the Opus API used for the clinical-trial dataset. This isolation was intended to prevent cross-article contamination, including the possibility that adverse-event severity assessments or demographic details from one article could influence the coding of another.

Each subagent returned a single structured JSON object containing both the extracted data and a mandatory rationale for every non-obvious or ambiguous coding decision, particularly adverse-event severity classifications that could not be determined unambiguously from the source text. Severity was coded on a fixed three-level scale, mild, moderate, or severe, adapted from the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) v5.0 and FDA seriousness criteria. The scale was modified to ensure that effects expected in the context of psychedelic-assisted therapy, such as transient anxiety or perceptual distortion, were not automatically classified as more severe than warranted. Completed extractions were subsequently merged using a separate deterministic script that enforced field-type, allowed-value, and internal-consistency checks across the dataset. The merge procedure was blocked if any article failed validation, ensuring that partially validated data were not carried forward into the final output tables.

### 2.2 Data cleaning, harmonization, and missing-data handling

Binary variables were coded on a four-level scheme: 1 (yes/present), 0 (no/absent), 3 (not applicable), and missing (not reported). In accordance with the USPSTF interpretive convention, missing and non-applicable values were treated as not met when quantifying the proportion of studies satisfying each indicator; this yields a conservative gap estimate that does not credit studies for unreported methodology. The raw data was processed through a Python pipeline to ensure consistency across the datasets, which included data extraction, categorization, and organization.

## Part 3: Comparison with USPSTF methodological standards, net benefits, screening framework, and Grade A/B benchmarks

### 3.1 Methodological evaluation

Descriptive statistics were conducted in Python to characterize the extent to which the resulting dataset aligns with the evidentiary standards of prevention science across five domains: methodology, benefits, harms, applicability, and certainty.

Each of the 44 included studies, comprising 33 alcohol studies, 4 smoking studies, and 7 opioid studies, was assigned to either Tier 1 or Tier 2\. Studies were classified as Tier 1 only when they reported a statistic that could be mathematically converted into a standardized between-groups effect size, specifically Hedges’ g, using an established conversion formula and without requiring the calculation of a new statistical test not reported by the original authors. These 16 studies were placed on a common numeric scale and presented together in the forest plot, thereby allowing their effect magnitudes to be visually compared and, in principle, synthesized quantitatively. Studies were classified as Tier 2 when their reported results could not be converted to a standardized effect size on this common scale for one of the reasons described below, including the absence of a comparator arm, the absence of a reported test statistic, or the use of a statistic not reducible to a one-degree-of-freedom between-groups comparison. Rather than excluding these 28 studies from the review, we classified the direction and approximate magnitude of each effect on the basis of the information reported by the original authors, using categories such as negative, null, small positive, moderate positive, large positive, single-arm positive, or unclassifiable. Because these results were not expressed on a common poolable scale, they were displayed in a categorical plot rather than a forest plot.

For all Tier 1 studies, we attempted to convert each study’s reported inferential statistic into a standardized mean-difference effect size, beginning with Cohen’s d and subsequently applying the Hedges small-sample bias correction to obtain Hedges’ g. We did not compute new statistical tests from raw data when such tests were not reported by the original authors; instead, each conversion was based exclusively on a statistic provided in the source paper. The specific conversion rule depended on the type of statistic reported. When Cohen’s d or Hedges’ g was already reported, the value was used directly. When a study reported a one-way F statistic with one numerator degree of freedom, corresponding to a two-group comparison, we calculated d as 2 multiplied by the square root of F divided by the error degrees of freedom. When partial eta-squared was reported for a two-group comparison, we calculated d as 2 multiplied by the square root of eta-squared divided by one minus eta-squared. When a chi-square statistic with one degree of freedom was reported from a 2 × 2 group-by-outcome table, we first converted the statistic to phi by taking the square root of chi-square divided by total N, and then calculated d as 2 multiplied by phi divided by the square root of one minus phi-squared. When an odds ratio was reported, we applied the standard Hasselblad-Hedges logit-to-d conversion, calculating d as the natural logarithm of the odds ratio multiplied by the square root of 3 and divided by pi. When a risk ratio was reported, we applied the same log-based formula as an approximation, but only in cases where the outcome was relatively rare.

Each resulting d value was then bias-corrected to Hedges’ g using the correction factor J, such that g \= d × J, where J \= 1 − 3/(4df − 1\) and df \= total N − 2\. The sampling variance of g was estimated using the standard formula for a two-independent-groups design. When a study reported only the total sample size and did not provide separate arm sizes, we assumed equal group sizes (n1 \= n2 \= total N/2) for the purpose of estimating variance, because the required allocation information was otherwise unavailable. This simplifying assumption is noted in the figure legend..

### 3.2 Net benefits

Additionally, the study considered net benefits, a major consideration for USPSTF. Here, based upon our literature review, we included preliminary responses to the three central areas of inquiry addressed by the framework: 1\) Benefits: Do psychedelic-assisted interventions improve the behaviors that are known to cause mortality, morbidity, and other adverse health and social outcomes in adults who currently smoke, or have problematic use of alcohol or opioids?Do they provide co-benefits such as improved mental, physiological, or social health?  2\) Harms: Are adverse events or side effects associated with their use?  Here, we applied the definition of Adverse Events established in the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events, V.5 (CTCAE). 3\) Net benefits: do the benefits significantly outweigh the harms? Are benefits conferred equitably among the adult population?

### 3.3 Benchmarking

By drawing from USPSTF reports, we profiled the volume of evidence that formed the basis for a category A/B recommendation for a range of interventions that might prove analogous to psychedelics in terms of net benefits, including tobacco (US Preventive Services Task Force, 2021), cardiovascular disease (US Preventive Services Task Force, 2022), HIV/AIDS (US Preventive Services Task Force, 2019), alcohol (US Preventive Services Task Force, 2018), and opioid and other unhealthy drug use (US Preventive Services Task Force, 2020). For each, we catalogued the number of studies and participants, pooled effect sizes (with 95% confidence intervals, standardized as Hedges’ g statistics), and the USPSTF’s assessment of the certainty and magnitude of net benefit (high, moderate, or low, and substantial, moderate, small, or zero/negative, respectively). The USPSTF also accounts for the disease burden of the preventable condition under consideration when assessing evidence sufficiency. We profiled the disease burdens based upon standard considerations (DALYs, mortality) and differentiating characteristics (acuity of outcomes, societal impacts). The general body of psychedelic science was considered relative to these examples to posit which intervention’s volume of evidence could serve as a target or benchmark for a USPSTF review of psychedelic science.

# Results

1. ## Methodological Evaluation

   The literature search identified 82 relevant peer-reviewed studies of psychedelics: 44 clinical trials (33 alcohol, 7 opioid, 4 smoking) and 38 observational studies. Of the 38 observational studies, 28 targeted one of the three review conditions (14 alcohol, 11 opioid, 3 smoking), and 10 targeted psychedelic-assisted treatment or use outside those three conditions and could not be assigned to a single condition; see Table 2\. These classifications indicate that, among clinical trials in particular, specific drugs were relatively condition-bound. For smoking, 100% of trials used psilocybin. For alcohol trials, 39% used LSD, 24% psilocybin, another 24% used ketamine, and 12% used MDMA. For opioid trials, 57% used ibogaine, 29% used ketamine, and 14% used LSD. While multiple observational studies did so, no trials included ayahuasca, mescaline, or a combination of psychedelics.

   Because USPSTF prioritizes clinical trials, the analyses focused its methodological assessment on the 44 clinical trial publications (Supplemental Table S.1-Table of all included studies). Table 3 details the indicators that address USPSTF methodological considerations, organized by this study across five domains, as follows:

   ***Study Identification & Design*** indicators varied across conditions. Across all 6 domains, no study met all criteria. 61% of trials involved randomization of participants to an active arm or a comparator, and was higher in opioid (71%) and alcohol (64%) trials than in tobacco trials (25%). Participant blinding was reported in 50% of trials; whereas 71% of opioid trials utilized blinding, no tobacco studies did (0%). Similarly, double-blinding was used in 57% of opioid trials, and was absent in tobacco studies. A caveat is that successful blinding of psychedelic studies is notoriously difficult, and functional unblinding rates are typically high (van Elk and Fried 2023).

   While 77% of all trials used validated outcome measurement scales, 100% of tobacco studies did so compared to 73% for alcohol and 86% for opioids. Only 18% of the total sample reported the results of power calculations. Importantly, only two (5%) of all trials included any interface with primary care settings (Grabski, 2022; Prior, 2014\), which is required for a USPSTF recommendation, which is likely partially due to lack of FDA approval.

   ***Population & Generalizability*** indicators were a primary deficiency. Baseline severity was reported in 89% of trials overall. However, tobacco studies lacked this characterization (0%). Female representation averaged 29% overall (alcohol 32%; opioids 13%; tobacco 36%), while BIPOC representation was highest in opioid trials (51%) compared to alcohol (20%) and tobacco (8%). Only 20% of trials recruited a participant pool reflective of real-world community or primary care populations. Moreover, inclusion of low-SES participants was limited (23% overall), with tobacco studies indicating the highest concentration at 75%.

   ***Intervention and Safety*** indicators varied. 100% of trials included description of the intervention, which involved therapeutic support in 100% of tobacco and alcohol and 43% of opioid studies. Overall, 80% of trials provided a summary of adverse events (100% tobacco; 86% of opioid; 76% of alcohol studies).

   ***Equity & Cultural Framing*** indicators showed that across all 44 trials, measurement of equity and cultural framing (e.g., racial/historical trauma) was absent, with 0% of studies including cultural context, Indigenous frameworks, or reciprocity for marginalized grou

   ***Outcomes & Follow-up*** indicators varied in terms of constructs and focus. Complete cessation was reported in 70% of studies, including 100% of tobacco studies. Relapse was tracked in 86% of opioid trials and 50% in tobacco, but only 33% of alcohol studies. Although 75% of tobacco studies measured physical/biological outcomes, for opioid (29%) and alcohol (30%) it was less. Measurement of implementation outcomes (23%), quality of life (16%) and mortality (5%) remained low across the entire sample.

2. ## Net benefits

   The USPSTF ultimately makes its assessment in terms of net benefits and net magnitude, weighing risks against gains. Figures 2A and B illustrate that the effect sizes of psychedelic-interventions to-date are consistent, large, and positive. The majority of trials (77%) reported improvement in problematic substance use (tobacco: 100%; opioids: 86%; alcohol: 73%).  In contrast, only XX% of clinical trial studies had participants who experienced serious adverse events. The 38 observational studies identified in this assessment totaled approximately 979,865 participants (58,481 if excluding Jones et al. 2022a, 2022b, and 2025\) compared to 2,338 in the 44 clinical trials. 84.2% of these report positive effects and 15.8% (6/38) reported the occurrence of at least 1 participant experiencing a serious adverse event; see Table 4\.

3. ## Benchmarking

   The USPSTF is guided by methodological standards held in common across interventions. However, the body of literature constituting the underlying evidence varies by intervention. Specifically, the number of studies and participants it takes to receive an A or B rating differs by intervention because the USPSTF focuses on the certainty and magnitude of net benefit over a set “volume” of data (Barry, 2023). Table 5 compares several pharmaceutical or substance-use interventions that received a Category A or B rating from the USPSTF to roughly benchmark the data volume needed for a preventive psychedelic intervention recommendation.

   While our assessment is only directional, not definitive, it points toward HIV PrEP as a possible benchmark for psychedelic interventions due to similarities in terms of large observed effect sizes, the absence of preventive measures presenting near-term risks for serious negative health outcomes and large societal burdens, and surrounding stigma. With a smaller number of studies and total participants, a PrEP benchmark is also more attainable in a shorter timespan. 

   # Discussion

   	Employing a public health lens and “policy backward” framework, this study evaluated the developments needed to produce a forward-facing research agenda capable of generating a USPSTF-relevant nomination and Category A/B recommendation for psychedelics as a preventive intervention. No study examined in this sample met all USPSTF-aligned indicators. This finding underscores the current gap between experimental research and the evidentiary standards required for preventive service recommendations by the USPSTF. 

   Even so, this study demonstrates that USPSTF prevention-oriented evidentiary standards are not yet fully met by psychedelic science. Even so, there is promising alignment with the USPSTF net benefit framework and an attainable evidentiary benchmark. In other words, these findings suggest that it is feasible to build a body of evidence that meets the standards required by the USPSTF to establish the net benefits of preventive psychedelic interventions with reliable certainty. So far, the effect sizes of psychedelic-intervention are consistently large and positive, with few participants across the studies reporting serious adverse events. The literature supports this net benefit profile, finding that, regardless of clinical intent, in controlled settings, psychedelic interventions (classic psychedelics in particular) are relatively safe, characterized by infrequent, and usually mild-to-moderate adverse events (Hinkle, 2024; Yerubandi, 2024; Freitus, 2025). In the first year of Oregon Psilocybin Services operations, adverse events \- behavioral or medical \- that required facilitator intervention beyond normal support, medical provider contact, or emergency services were rare, with annual rates of 2.42 and 2.79 per 1,000 sessions, respectively (Yu, 2026). As of June 2026, according to OHA’s Q12026 records, total adverse events, including post-session, are recorded at 0.33% more than 22,000 people served, and only 32 (0.15%) of sessions involved calls to emergency services. 

   	This study elucidates important action items to bridge this evidentiary gap.  In particular, limited trial participation from populations more representative of the general adult primary care population and low frequency of primary care integration (5%) into the study designs fail the USPSTF external validity criteria, highlighting a research gap. This gap is not surprising since early psychedelic clinical trials focused on safety and efficacy, with limited consideration of not only acute psychedelic drug effects on an individual basis, but also of how such treatments could scale to population levels (DellaCrosse et al., 2024). 

   We acknowledge that there are important methodological limitations and generalizability concerns related to the current evidence base for psychedelic-assisted interventions, including the small sample sizes of most existing trials, narrow target populations, and functional unblinding. However, a number of phase 2-3 clinical trials are underway in large, heterogeneous populations ([ClinicalTrials.gov](http://ClinicalTrials.gov) 2026 a/b), and methodological limitations are receiving attention from government funders (NIH RFA-MH-27-135). This growing investment in larger, better-powered, and more rigorously designed trials suggests that many of the evidentiary gaps identified here are addressable. Supplementing evidence from these trials with large observational studies can help identify downstream impacts on prevention targets.

   Equity considerations are increasingly emphasized by USPSTF, signalling that they should similarly rise in importance in psychedelic research design. This is another case for investment in participant pools more reflective of the general, or primary care, population. Also within this objective, cultural framing and reciprocity for Indigenous communities (important given Western psychedelic science is built upon millennia of Indigenous stewardship of sacred plant medicines) could be included as they represent best public health practice, and because their inclusion would be important to repair and reciprocity. 

   Additionally, current psychedelic research is limited in its ability to achieve a USPSTF Grade A or B recommendation because it does not yet adequately reflect the populations and settings where preventive services are usually delivered. In our review, only 20% of clinical trials recruited participants representative of real-world community or primary care populations, only 23% included low socioeconomic status (SES) participants, average female participation was 29%, average BIPOC participation was 21%, and only 5% of studies had any interaction within primary care settings. No studies used cultural framing, Indigenous frameworks, or reciprocity principles.

   To address these gaps, greater investment in trials is needed in order to recruit participants representative of the primary care populations and populations most affected by tobacco, alcohol, and opioid use disorders, including racially and ethnically diverse communities, rural populations, uninsured and Medicaid patients, and individuals with lower socioeconomic status. Recruitment could be facilitated by embedding studies within primary care and community health settings, thereby also increasing relevancy to the USPSTF.

   ## Limitations

   There are several limitations of this study. The first pertains to the data in terms of the incompleteness of the indicators and the focus on individual studies. An actual USPSTF review would be more comprehensive and grapple with a dynamic comparison of different studies, with an emphasis on pooled/meta/summary studies. Furthermore, the AI-based extraction process may have led to errors and misinterpretation of codes. Even so, the present study is sufficient to demonstrate the relevance of a psychedelic prevention framework and point toward design areas to prioritize in targeting prevention in psychedelic science. 

   Nevertheless, given the large effect sizes and population health potential seen in psychedelic research to-date, there is merit to developing an evidence base that can expand psychedelic coverage opportunities. Establishing psychedelic intervention to be preventive of preclinical health changes and adverse health outcomes is a key pathway to access and to population health and equity. This approach mirrors the Grade A tobacco cessation precedent, where cessation in current smokers is treated as prevention against downstream chronic diseases (USPSTF, 2021a). 

   A starting point is for the design of research to incorporate the evidentiary standards of the USPSTF and to ensure that public and private investment in this research is sufficiently matched, especially to improve participant profile and applicability to the primary care context. To support prevention claims, psychedelic clinical trials should also extend follow-up windows to capture change in disease and behavior progression, including tracking overdose,suicide/suicidality, and substance use disorder-related morbidity and mortality. Additionally, behavior change effect sizes could be modelled onto established SUD-related disease trajectories to estimate averted adverse outcomes and associated costs. See for example, the Marseilles, et al. (2026) assessment of cost-efficacy pertaining to psychedelic prevention of smoking-related adverse health outcomes.

   In addition to expanding the frame of psychedelic science to incorporate preventive care, there are two major conceptual contributions made by this assessment that warrant highlighting as avenues for advancing a prevention pathway to expanded access. 

   ## 

   ## 1\. Primary care compatibility 

   The USPSTF specifically addresses prevention within a primary care context in terms of service delivery and populations served. Psychedelic-assisted therapy has been developed almost exclusively within psychiatry or mental health service models, but this may not be the optimal, or most equitable, home for it at scale. Psychiatry is less accessible than primary care, carries higher costs, and has historically focused on treatment rather than prevention. Meanwhile, primary care providers already shoulder a substantial proportion of mental health care in the US, filling gaps created by psychiatric workforce shortages and insurance barriers. This existing role makes primary care a natural fit for psychedelic medicine.

   Several features of psychedelic interventions specifically favor a primary care model. These compounds produce significant acute physiologic effects, including elevations in blood pressure and heart rate, that require clinical monitoring and risk stratification. Primary care clinicians, who routinely assess cardiovascular risk, are well-positioned to conduct pre-treatment screening and provide medical oversight during sessions. At the same time, the therapy components of psychedelic treatment do not require a physician: the preparation, session support, and integration work that drive therapeutic outcomes are well within the scope of co-located behavioral health providers such as social workers and marriage and family therapists, or even non-clinical state-certified facilitators.

   A collaborative care model, in which a primary care physician provides medical oversight and a non-physician behavioral health or other provider conducts the therapeutic work, is not only clinically coherent but economically compelling. Such a collaborative approach is well-established within primary care, closely aligning with the Screening, Brief Intervention, and Referral to Treatment (SBIRT) framework, and is already under consideration by the USPSTF for unhealthy alcohol use in adults and adolescents (USPSTF, 2025b). In this existing model, primary care physicians oversee screening and medical stratification, while co-located behavioral health clinicians provide the counseling and facilitate necessary care transitions. Psychedelic-assisted interventions could utilize a parallel workflow, where primary care physicians manage pre-treatment assessments and safety monitoring, leaving the preparation, session facilitation, and therapeutic integration to behavioral health specialists or other trained facilitators and preparation/integration providers. This structure allows the physician to serve in a supervisory and on-call capacity while containing costs and expanding capacity and access.

   There is also a representational argument. Primary care practices and co-located behavioral health teams tend to reflect the demographics of the communities they serve more closely, and also are present in tribal communities. Delivering psychedelic therapy through these settings could improve cultural competence, reduce therapeutic mistrust, and generate efficacy data in more diverse and generalizable populations.

   Research design should follow this logic. Studies should test models in which medical screening and oversight are provided by primary care physicians and therapeutic support is provided by non-physician behavioral health clinicians. Family medicine and general internal medicine departments should actively support faculty research in psychedelic medicine.

   ## 2\. Observational studies and state-regulated programs of elevated significance in USPSTF consideration of psychedelics 

   Additionally, there is merit in increasing the stature of psychedelic observational studies and state registries, with large and diverse study populations, in USPSTF deliberations and other coverage decisions. Observational studies may play a larger role in evidence generation for psychedelic prevention research than is typical for other interventions. A significant benefit of observational studies and registries is the possibility of monitoring adverse events / risks on a mass scale. This priority is echoed in the recent FDA guidance on psychedelics (USFDA, 2026). Observational studies are more reflective of the settings where the significant majority of psychedelics will be consumed, regardless of their regulatory status. Far more people have had exposure to psychedelics than is common for novel compounds seeking regulatory approval; an estimated 11 million US adults took psilocybin in the past year alone (RAND, 2025). In the case of psychedelics, observational and registry data sets may be well-suited to meet USPSTF criteria for net benefits, net magnitude, external validity and equity. Further, as illustrated in Table 4, above, there are no drug interventions recommended by USPSTF for prevention of AUD or OUD, indicating high unmet need, especially given, for example, the urgency of the opioid crisis and the high portion of current smokers who want to quit (Babb, 2017), making the profiles offered by observational studies more salient.

   State psychedelic program data also represent a significant opportunity to accelerate development of the evidence base needed for USPSTF approval. While Schedule I status restricts commercial distribution and prescribing, it does not preclude systematic evaluation, surveillance, or public health monitoring of state-legal activities. The nascent regulatory structures in Oregon, Colorado, and other states therefore offer a critical policy opportunity to establish comprehensive, real-world surveillance and evaluation systems that provide the scale of data the field requires and the USPSTF needs for its determinations. 

   For example, although Oregon Psilocybin Services (OPS) is designed as a non-medical wellness model requiring no diagnosis (Yu, 2026), a substantial portion of participants report motivations that align with conditions managed in psychiatry and primary care, such as anxiety, depression, PTSD, and substance use disorders (Yu, 2026). Consequently, a significant share of this "non-medical" population is de facto treatment-seeking, accessing care outside conventional clinical or insurance-based frameworks. This presents an opportunity to track safety and estimate net benefits, if changes in behaviors that can prevent adverse health outcomes under real-world conditions are monitored.

   Capitalizing on this opportunity necessitates ensuring not only that state-licensed service centers capture key prevention and health promotion measures, including mental health trajectories, substance use and other behavioral or lifestyle patterns, the associated health outcomes, and healthcare utilization. These metrics should be standardized, compatible with existing state health priorities and metrics such as reflected in State Health Improvement Plans (SHIPs), and link to county-level data. Such integration would scale the psychedelic evidence base through the broader prevention and population health monitoring architecture. State- academic partnerships could facilitate ensuring the evidentiary standards for prevention are met, standardize outcome measurement, and extend follow-up beyond the acute session, generating insights on net benefits and prevention through longitudinal, real-world safety and effectiveness data that surpasses current clinical trials and aggregate state dashboards.

   Furthermore, this infrastructure carries direct implications for equitable access, for example by opening the opportunity for care regardless of insurance coverage or psychiatric service availability. States that implement credible monitoring systems are also better positioned to advocate for expanded coverage and reimbursement through Medicaid waivers, state employee health plans, or private insurer negotiations. 

   # Conclusion and Path Forward

   To our knowledge, this study is the first public health-informed review aimed at outlining a viable policy pathway toward access to preventive psychedelic care. Just as the feasibility of integrating psychedelic care into substance use disorder treatment models has been positively assessed (Yaden, 2024), so too can it be considered for primary care-based preventive care. 

   To do so, will involve prioritization and investment that enables overcoming or circumventing the limitations and internal validity threats frequently encountered in psychedelic trials (Weleff, 2025). It also requires that research and investment place greater emphasis on external validity, follow-up duration, primary care settings, and psychedelic interventions targeted at earlier points in the progression of problematic substance use trajectories. In the United States (US), pursuant to Executive Order 14207, "Accelerating Medical Treatments for Serious Mental Illness," coordination throughout the US Department of Health and Human Services to incorporate and prioritize prevention standards for psychedelic science could produce significant gains. If coordinated globally, a funded research agenda prioritizing the methodological standards for preventive care could even more rapidly scale psychedelic interventions from clinical breakthroughs to expanded preventive services for improved population health.
